blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Class unlearning for video segmentation aims to ensure that a removed category cannot be reconstructed from a deployed model's outputs. Current leakage evaluation algorithms inspect one frame at a time, and we show that this understates leakage by a wide margin: an attacker that averages a model's output field over a two-second clip recovers the forgotten class from every method we evaluate on VSPW and most on Virtual KITTI~2, including models whose per-frame predictions are visually indistinguishable from a retrain oracle (a model trained from scratch without the forgotten class). We attribute the recoverable signal to cross-frame redundancy rather than object trajectory, establish this with a time-shuffled control that leaves leakage intact, and introduce PACE, an unlearning method that suppresses redundancy directly using an exactly permutation-invariant pooled adversarial discriminator and a two-sided temporal consistency objective. Across VSPW and Virtual KITTI~2, PACE lowers pooled attacker AP to $18.79$ (\texttt{person}) and $12.10$ (\texttt{car}) on VSPW and $9.11$ (\texttt{car}) on Virtual KITTI~2, achieving on the latter the strongest suppression among verdict-safe methods retaining usable utility, while retaining $19.8$ mIoU on VSPW \texttt{car} against at most $8.3$ for any baseline achieving comparable erasure.

blocks.en:
Our core contributions are three-fold: • A sound audit for video unlearning. We show that per-frame
verification systematically understates recoverable information, and
introduce a time-shuffled control that decomposes a temporal attacker’s
advantage into redundancy and trajectory terms, establishing redundancy
as the operative channel across architectures, spans, classes,
and datasets. • An order-invariant adversarial objective. We introduce
PACE, whose pooled adversarial discriminator is exactly permutation-invariant by
construction rather than by training, paired with a two-sided consistency
term that removes the frozen-region solution of one-sided formulations. • Strongest suppression at usable accuracy, on two datasets. PACE attains the lowest pooled leakage of any verdict-safe method that
retains usable utility, across both VSPW classes and on Virtual KITTI 2;
on VSPW, PACE and PACE-T are the only methods combining complete
per-frame erasure with useful utility, where all baselines reaching
comparable erasure fall to 8.3 8.3 mIoU or below.

blocks.en:
Exact unlearning consists of retraining on the retained data, either directly or through
sharding that limits how much of the model must be rebuilt [ 3 , 1 ] . Because full retraining is costly
at video scale, practical approaches instead modify a trained model so that it
behaves as though the forgotten set were absent. These include gradient ascent
on the forget set and stabilized variants [ 42 , 22 ] ; Fisher- and
influence-based parameter scrubbing [ 19 , 20 , 18 ] ;
saliency-restricted updates [ 13 ] ; selective
dampening [ 14 ] ; teacher–student objectives that repel the
forget set while preserving the retain set [ 30 , 9 ] ; and relabeling with an explicit
substitute target [ 41 , 5 ] .

Most of these methods were developed and evaluated on image classification,
where each sample is observed once, so their verification procedures
inherit a single-sample observation model. Forget-set accuracy alone
is not a sufficient certificate of forgetting [ 17 ] , while
membership-inference attacks provide a stronger test of residual information [ 39 , 4 ] . Weak evaluations can
create a false sense of privacy [ 25 ] , and the first NeurIPS
unlearning competition showed that method rankings can change with the
evaluation protocol [ 44 ] . These
works strengthen the attacker’s inference procedure while keeping its
observation window fixed at one sample. Our setting changes the observation
window itself: a video model exposes a sequence of correlated outputs that
can be jointly analyzed. To our knowledge, prior work has not evaluated
video segmentation unlearning against a temporal pooling attacker, nor
separated the order-dependent and redundancy-based components of the
recovered signal.

beyond the nominal prediction task [ 15 , 48 , 27 ] , and neural networks
can encode attributes that they were not explicitly trained to predict [ 40 ] . Our attacker is related to this line of work,

individual frame and becomes recoverable only after aggregation across
correlated observations: repeated-query amplification, where the attacker
gains from the redundancy in multiple outputs of the same scene.

Suppressing information by training a representation against a discriminator
that attempts to recover it is well established, from domain-adversarial
learning [ 16 ] through censored
representations [ 12 ] and controllable
invariance [ 46 ] . The same adversarial formulation has
been used for privacy-preserving recognition and anonymization [ 38 , 45 , 10 ] and for learned
redaction [ 36 ] . These approaches suppress the
information accessible to the particular discriminator they employ. Our
setting differs in that the relevant leakage mechanism is first identified
empirically, and the discriminator is then constrained to observe that
quantity—the time-averaged output—making permutation invariance a
property of the attack surface rather than a behavior to be learned. The generator’s completion behavior is also related
to context-based inpainting [ 37 , 47 ] ,
although our objective is non-recoverability of a forgotten class rather than
perceptual plausibility.

the latter with 5 × 5\times fewer parameters than the 3D model, so any difference
reflects receptive field rather than capacity.

blocks.zh: 6 结论

blocks.en:
Per-frame verification does not bound what an attacker recovers from a
video segmentation model: averaging a two-second clip recovers the forgotten
class from popular unlearning methods we evaluated on VSPW and most on Virtual KITTI 2,
including models whose per-frame predictions are indistinguishable from a
retrain oracle. A time-shuffled control then identifies redundancy, not
trajectory, as the carrier, across three attacker architectures, two spans,
two classes, and two datasets.
